Yeah, baby.

So, yeah, Steve, this is a real milestone.  This is one of the pieces of technology that I've been waiting for for a long time.  This is the beginning of real augmented reality.  To give you a quick definition of what augmented reality is:  so imagine a car mechanic that's wearing a pair of sunglasses and a computer is projecting onto the inside of those sunglasses a schematic so that the car mechanic is looking at the car engine and the computer's projecting say, the wiring system.  So wherever he turns his head, the, it'll look like it's in 3D so he can see, or he or she can see things that aren't actually visible to the naked eye because the computer is laying that on top of reality.  It's like another layer, or putting layers of information on top of reality.  Or, a surgeon performing open-heart surgery would be able to see the heart in a 3D view unobstructed by the rest of the tissue surrounding it, or the rib cage, or whatever.  You know, having that vantage point gives people the opportunity to achieve things much faster, more precisely and with much greater success overall.  Now, I'm not saying that Google glass is offering that to us right now, but what Google is offering is the very first step in true augmented reality.  So let me give you a quick list of the features of what it is, and I'll describe to you the actual component that you're wearing is, it's like taking a pair of sunglasses, removing the lenses and then on one side, on one eye, they'll put a, it's like a little module there that has a piece of glass that's hovering in front of one of your eyes.  It'll project into your vision onto that piece of glass you're looking through that piece of glass, one of your eyes.  It'll project a computer screen that looks like it's floating three or four feet in front of you, that doesn't have any borders or anything of course.  And there's simply information there.  You know, there's text, there's however, they're showing this information, it's gonna be a varying degree of different things.  And you're gonna be talking to it.  You're not gonna be using keyboard or a mouse or anything, that you're primarily gonna be using vocalization to turn it on, to tell it what you need it to do.  And some of the features that it's launching with are it's gonna be able to record video.  What you see, it's gonna record.  It's gonna take pictures.  You're gonna be able to start Google-Plus hangouts with people.  You're gonna be able to search.  You're gonna be able to also search photos, which is cool.  You're gonna be able to do translations, you're gonna be able to get directions; you're gonna be able to use the Google Now software, which is like iPhone's Siri, where you can ask more complicated questions and actually tell it to do certain things, like take notes, put something in my address book, in my calendar, whatever.  You can send messages to people and you can get flight, or there'll be a flight detail database attached, so you can call that up when you need it.  You would start each command with "Okay, Glass," as if you were talking to someone.  "Okay, Glass, I want you to start recording video right now."  "Okay, Glass, stop recording video."  The really cool thing about this though, is you take it with you, it connects into your iPhone or to your Android operating system, and it is based off of the Android operating system.  And you wear it and you just put it on and you forget that it's there and it just becomes another interface for you.   The big thing here is, guys, it truly is the beginning of the next way that we're gonna be interacting and experiencing reality.  And it's going to be augmented by computers in a way now that we've really never experienced it before.  We're all gonna be able to do things that we normally wouldn't be able to do, even simple things.  Like let's say you went to Ikea and you bought a bookshelf.  Everybody knows that directions that come from companies like Ikea or whatever, some are better than other, but for the most part having to construct something is a complete and total pain in the ass.  This would be showing you what to do.  It would be giving you visual cues using the actual things that you're looking at.  Like, showing you what pieces connect to each other and where.

And that's the key, Jay.  To me that's the key.  It's contextual information.  It's not, you're not just surfing web pages.  You are seeing overlays on reality and it knows what you're looking at, and gives you information based on your environment and what you're interacting with.  And that's one of the reasons why this is gonna be so powerful.
All right, Bob, Bob, what would be the porn application?
Oh, my god.  Don't even go there.
God.  Come on.
Well, Bob's talking about what it will be like down the road, and
I have to talk about that.

Maybe a future use of this would be that you could tell Google glass "When I'm sitting at my work desk, I want my monitor to appear as if it's here where a physical monitor would be" but when you turn your head away, it stays in that three-dimensional space; you know, if you're looking at your computer monitor and you turn your head to the left, you don't see the monitor anymore, you wouldn't in real life.
Exactly.
Now let me be the wet-blanket skeptic.
(laughing) I was gonna mention something about that.

To bring things down a little bit.  So everything that you guys are saying may come to pass at some point, but the thing that we have to keep in mind is that until we put this technology in the hands of lots of people, it's really hard to predict how people will want to use it.
Oh, absolutely.

And what it will be useful for.  So all the things that you guys are speculating about, are speculation.  So we don't know if this is going to be the smart phone, where everyone's gonna want to have 'em and it's gonna be much more useful than anyone ever thought, or if it's gonna be the Segue.  You know, where it's not gonna be so revolutionary.  But it'll have a niche where people use it for certain specific things, or, guys, remember the high-definition, high-frame rate situation where there just was something annoying about it, that people have a hard time adapting to.
Ah, you're so full of it
Yeah, adaptation.

That's a horrible analogy.  (laughter)  Because this, this isn't, it's not a segue.  People were gonna build cities around segue.  That was a ridiculous prediction.  It's  not like a segue at all.  This is an improvement on the computer interfaces.  I mean computer interfaces, they're not going anywhere.  That's a proven technology.  It's just another way, it's another type of monitor, Steve.

I know, Bob.  I'm just saying, until people start using we won't know, it's like a video phone.  We talked about the fact, oh video phones are coming.  Well, why wouldn't you use a video phone?  And it turns out that for a lot of things you don't wanna be looking at somebody.  Why is texting so popular?  The use of technology is hard to predict.
I agree.
All right, well, Evan.  Tell us about last week's Who's That Noisy?
I'll do one better and play for you last week's Who's That Noisy?  Who could forget this, this wonderful little sound.  Here we go.
Bird-like tweeting. The tweet song is repeated several times, pretty much the same each time.
Definitely not a bird, definitely not a plane.
What is it?
Superman.  (laughs)  That is . . . the whistlepig.
The whistlepig.
(laughing) The whistlepig.
(numerous garbled comments)
What the hell is a whistlepig?
A groundhog!
Remember, from Groundhog's Day?
We only covered it a few weeks ago.
That's an actual pig?
No, it's a groundhog.  The whistlepig is another name for the groundhog.

Right.  Woodchuck, is another name for the groundhog.  Some people call it a land beaver.  And they're all over the place, especially in North America.  Very common in northeastern parts of the continent, and in the central United States.  Several guesses; only a few correct answers this week came in to us.  Congratulations to Wayne Heller.  Your name was drawn.  You are the winner this week.  You're in the drawing for the end-of-the-year contest by which we will put all names in the hat from the week winners and that grand-prize winner will join us on the SGU to play a round of Science or Fiction.  All right, so.  You guys ready for this week?
Always.
Yes.
It is another noisy we have this week.  It's short.  Here we go:

Men's voices speaking on some kind of communicators:
Person 1:  You're looking a little hot and all your calls will be a little early.  (Beep)  Person 2:  Okay.  Person 3:  And that looks good here.
Isn't that when they made the Six-Million-Dollar Man, and he was about to crash?  No?
That's an interesting guess, Jay.  No, that's not correct.
I hope at some point in my life I'm gonna be talking to someone and that whistle will comment like the
That call-tone?
Yeah, I love that.

What I would like to see in the answer for this week is not a generic idea of what you think the noise is.  I would like to know pretty exactly where you recognize that noise from.  Send us your guess.  wtn@theskepticsguide.org; that's the email address for Who's That Noisy submissions.  Or you can post it on our forums, sguforums.com.  Every week I wish you all the best of
(shouting) Good luck everybody!
Thank you, Jay.  (laughter)
I was getting very excited, Evan.
All right, we have one question this week.  This comes from Joe Shoults.  And this is the shortest question we 've ever had.
The answer is six inches.
Four foot one.
Joe writes "Why do we say "ow"?
Wow!  What a good question!  Holy crap!
Steve, can I try to answer it and see if I'm anywhere near correct?
You can try.
Okay.
The first thing that occurred to me when I read that email when it came in was, well, first, the word is cultural.  I'm sure that in other cultures they don't say "ow," they say other things.
Are you sure?
I'm guessing.  I'm guessing.
That's my guess as well.
The other thing is I think we're giving a cue to the other mammals around us that we're injured.
Here's my guess.  My guess is ow is short for ouch.
Why do we say ouch?
'Cause ouch is short for ouch-a-daisy.
(laughter)
He didn't say "why do we say ouch?"; that wasn't the question.  Said "why do we say 'ow'?"  (laughter)
Don't split hairs.  Why do we make a vocalization when we get hurt?
Do you think there's any published scientific research that might enlighten us on that question?
I'm sure you know.
If there is, you have it, Steve.

All of the evolutionary psychological answers, there's no answer to that.  (laughter)  This is all hand waving.  We don't know.  No one knows.  You could make up any kind of plausible sounding answer that you like for that.
So I'm right!

The answer is we don't know.  That's what the answer is.  But I did look at this from a couple of angles, just to see what I could find.  One was, 'cause I remember reading this study but I wanted just to see what all the literature was, about swearing and pain perception.  I couldn't find anything published about saying "ow" or "ouch," but I could find swearing.  And, the research does show that if you swear when you have, like stub your toe, or have physical pain, that your perception of the pain is decreased.  It does help.
Wow.
However, get this, if you swear all the time, then the benefit of swearing goes down.
Fuck that!
'Cause you've numbed yourself.
I could see that.
Yeah, so you have to keep your swearing in reserve for when you stub your toe.
Save it for the pain.
Save it for the pain.
How 'bout, now, what about instead of physical pain, what about emotional pain?

Yeah, well, we also use it in lots of related ways, like, when somebody says something bad that happened, you might say, "ooo, ouch" as a way of saying, expressing sympathy or if somebody insults you really bad you might say "ouch" like sarcastically.  Try to say like, oh you hurt me.  I also had the same question, what is the, how international or cross-cultural is "ow" or "ouch."  So I looked it up.   Here's a smattering of what other cultures say instead of ouch.  Ayee.  So "ayee" or "ow" are the two main things that cultures say.   In French, "ayee"; Thai, "oi"; Spanish, "ai"; Polish, "ouch"; Maltese, "ach"; Iran, "ai" or "ach" or "oof"; Afghanistan, "oof"; Germany, it's a-u-a, "Aua"; Dutch is "ow"; Norwegian, "ow"; Danish, it says a-v, I'm not sure if that's supposed to also be pronounced "ow";
Probably.
Chinese, the only two-syllable one I came across, "ayo" or "ayah"; Turkish, "ach" or "ai"; so very similar across the cultures.  It's mainly a lot of "ai" "ach" "oof" "ow."  Very similar.
That's interesting, too, and they're all short.
A lot of a's, o's, yeah, they're all short.  The Chinese one was the only one I found that was two syllables.
Very cool.  That's so interesting.  I love that.
Interview with Jon Ronson, recorded at CSICon 2012.
sections.title: Interview with Jon Ronson

sections.text: All right, we have a very interesting interview that we recorded last October at CSICon with Jon Ronson.
(Music)
We're sitting here now with Jon Ronson.   Jon, welcome back to the Skeptics' Guide.
It's good to be back.  Thank you , Steve.  And it's nice to meet you all after I've heard 400 episodes of you.
Wow.
Only 381.
Jon, I believe you owe us an apology.

I do.  Last time I was on, it was to talk about my book The Psychopath Test and it was on my birthday.  And it was quite late, it was like 11:00 at night.  And unlike me, I was drunk.  And I, it turns out that I am a befuddled and slightly angry drunk.
'Cause we couldn't tell the difference.
(garbled comments and laughter)
When I listened back I was ashamed.  I was ashamed.  Mid-sentence I would drift off.  I didn't know what I was talking about.
We said "Jon was sharp as ever tonight, wasn't he?"
(laughter)

Well, actually, after the podcast, I accidentally typed my name into Google and I saw somebody saying "God, Jon Ronson sounded weird on Skeptics' Guide."  (laughter)  But the reason why was because it was my birthday and I'd been out with my family and I was drunk.
I don't think you told us it was your birthday.
Yeah, it was my birthday.  Yeah.
Warn us next time, okay?
Yes.
(laughter)
But yes, you can see now I'm as sharp as a pin.
Yes.
Absolutely.
Ouch!
Pithy.  Much more pithy.
Pithy as a pin.
So, Jon, can you please say to me:  (in a English accent) "But of course I was drunk at the time."
(laughter)
I don't talk like that.  Like somebody, like a buffoon from Downton Abbey.  (laughter)
Now you sound like the first of the reboot of the Doctors Who.
Right.  The Doctors Who.
(garbled comments)
It was, what was the actor's name?  Not David Tennant.
Christopher Eccleston?
Yeah, Christopher Eccleston.  What kind of accent does he have?  Northern.
Yeah, I believe he's from the Northeast.  I see him jogging maniacally in a park in North London.
You do?
Yeah, he's a big jogger.
Interesting.
Maniacal.  Like he's really running away something.   (laughter)
Demons . . .
May be.
Personal demons . . .
Yeah, or . . . Daleks.  "(laughter)
Jon, what are you working on now?

Now I'm starting to write a new book on the subject . . . I don't want to talk too much about it because I don't wanna talk it all out.  It always helps me to kind of internalize the thing that I'm writing about.   It's kind of on the subject of humiliation.  I always like to start with a word.  So The Psychopath Test the word, I guess, was "madness."  About how madness is a more powerful engine in our lives than rationality.  And in The Men Who Stare at Goats I guess the word was a phrase, and it was "irrationality at the heart of power."  And Them was like, paranoia at the fringes of society, and the new word is "humiliation."  I'm very interested.  I was really surprised, actually, I've just brought out this collection called Lost at Sea, and I was reading it; it's an audiobook, and I was amazed at fifteen years of adventure stories, how often the subject of humiliation comes up.  How often people said to me, my greatest fear in life was being humiliated, and here it was coming true.  It seems to be a running theme in my stories.
And what about people who don't get humiliated?  Are there any people who just . . .
Well that's another interesting thing.  I mean, psychopaths don't get humilitated.
Meaning they're immune to humilitation.

I think so, yeah.  So it seems.  They get annoyed, as you know.  They get very cross if they feel slighted.  So they've got terrible grandiosity issues.  But, when they're caught in a lie, they don't feel bad about it.  That's one of _________________ big things, feeling unembarrassed about being caught lying.  But other people don't get humiliated, too.  And I'm really interested in those people.

It's interesting to think, is the most powerful source of humiliation for the average person being caught in a lie, or is it, like, a lot of people will do the default "oh, I'm naked in public, I would be humiliated."  That wouldn't bother me at all.
It would bother everyone else.
But I definitely think being caught in a social lie, when people know.  Especially like stealing somebody else's work type of lie, would be horrible.  That would be horrible, right?

JR;  I can't think of anything worse than being the recipient of some kind of storm like that.  Like Jonah Lehrer or Mike Daisey, those people.  To me that's like, that's the kind of thing that would wake me up sweating.

And there's so many people right now in what I feel is your field, in a way, like the people who are writing these sometimes slightly fictionalized accounts, but of truthful stories, you know, and David Sedaris went through this.  And it's kind of sad, like they're all people I love, and to see that happening. . .

Yeah, I feel a bit sorry for Jonah Lehrer, because his big crime was inflating Bob Dylan quotes.  Or, in fact, inventing them.  And as somebody pointed out in the wake of that storm, Bob Dylan's autobiography is full of made-up stuff.  Yet, nobody goes for Dylan.  It does feel slightly subjective.
Also, you know, sometimes you can't tell what Dylan's saying anyway.  (laughter)
Can't tell what he's singing.
Another thing that worried me was, before Jonah Lehrer got done for that, he was done for self-plagiarism.
Yeah.
And I . . . I've never . . .
What is self-plagiarism?
Well, it's basically using the same material like say in an article for the New Yorker and a blog for Wired.
Yeah.  Lifting like word-for-word, same paragraph, and dropping into a different article, usually.
When I heard that, I thought . . . so he wasn't stealing somebody else's work, he was repeating his own work.
Repeating his own.

And when I heard that, I thought, Frank Sinatra would sing My Way every night!  You know?  Is that the worst crime in the world?  I used to do that, and not worry.  If I had like a really great line, there's a line in The Psychopath Test where I say . . . yes, there's a line in The Psychopath Test where I say, I'm talking about how bankers weren't, were kind of ignored, like the wickedness of hedge-fund managers and stuff, was kind of ignored for a long time and they were getting away with it.  And I said the reason why they were getting away with it was because they were boring, and journalists don't like to write about boring people because the more colorful the prose, the better it looks for the journalist.  So I said if you want to get away with wielding true malevolent power, be boring.  And I'd actually written something very very similar to that a couple years ago in a column for the Guardian and it was completely ignored, and I thought, this is like a really interesting point.  So I was happy to give it another shot in The Psychopath Test.  And sure enough, it's become one of the more popular quotes in that book.
The problem with that, I mean, 'cause what else are you gonna say, every single time?  "As I once said."  I mean, no.
I was surprised actually, when that came up as an issue for Jonah, and it worried me that people were gonna start going for journalistic misdeeds too much.

Yeah, it becomes a witch hunt.  And I think some people are doing it because they can.  Because we have the technology, if you will, to sift through everything everyone's written.  I know Gerald Posner faced that, where someone thought that he had plagiarized part of his book.  And then somebody decided to cross reference everything he ever wrote with searching algorithms, where you could search everything he wrote and come up with all these other instances where lines from his research found their way into his books, or his articles without being properly referenced.  And he admitted, clearly my process has broken down here and I haven't been keeping track of where these lines were coming from.  So he admitted that inadvertently things have crept in, but I don't know who can withstand that kind of really thorough scrutiny.  I mean we all have things rattling around in our head that we heard from other people, and if you write a lot, that stuff is gonna end up in what you write.
Absolutely.  It did worry me.  It seems to be kind of drifting off a little bit now.  The funny thing about Mike Daisey, you know his story; he went to China and
Foxconn.

Yeah, to Foxconn, and was writing about the abuses that Foxconn were . . . everything he wrote was true.  But his grave error of judgment was he said he witnessed it all first-hand.  The tragedy of Mike Daisey is if he'd stayed in China for a couple of weeks longer, he could have actually got everything that he purported to get.  All he had to do was get on a few more planes and go and meet a few more people.  And it would have been the greatest expose of Apple of all time.  But he didn't.

But I think even if he had, though, he still would have messed with the narrative, because he, that was another huge thing; was not just that it didn't happen to him, but then he was screwing with the narrative not in a way that just makes better story arc but in a way that drastically altered events:  where they happened, how they happened.  And I feel like even if he had stayed there a few weeks; because what he is at heart is a storyteller, and that's what he values.  He doesn't value truth.
But isn't that the problem with journalism in general, is that ultimately it's a storytelling endeavor, and the truth, or the facts, becomes second in importance to that?

Well no, because it's possible, I think, to balance those things; to know how to take what you're seeing . . . it's like taking a photo.  You know, you could take a photo; I could take a photo of something out the window right now and then we could have a professional photographer come in and come up with something that's amazingly better.  We're both representing the truth, but one of us has a better eye for how to capture it.  It's exactly the same.

Well, I think a better analogy there would be then you take it onto to PhotoShop and maybe you color correct it a little bit, or you enhance the contrast.  Or then maybe you said, you know what, a tree instead of this building would work a little bit better.  That building's ugly.  I wanna put a tree there so that it doesn't ruin . . .
Well, yeah, that would be the  . . .  yeah.

And then there's a slippery slope.  I'm talking more about this slippery slope.  Of course all good journalism is storytelling.  You know, Jon, you know this obviously better than any of us, you're a journalist and an author.  You've written, obviously, you've listed your most recent successful books, screenplays, et cetera.  And you have to tell a good story.  But at the same time you're trying to convey an accurate portrayal of the subject matter.  But isn't there this temptation to always tweak it to make the story a little bit better, even if it's not exactly true?

Well, I always try and make it true.  And, a rather good thing about, you know, it's good to, it's, I feel sorry for the likes of Jonah Lehrer for being the one who's thrown into the bonfire.  But I guess a good thing about that is it does keep everybody in check.  But, I always try to keep a ___________, I have never been, nothing bad's ever happened, you know, I've never . . .
Yeah.  Yeah, yeah.

You know, so I've always been all right.  Yeah, but you think about this every time you write something.  It's really important.  I always think it's the fact that I suffer from anxiety that stops me from transgressing.  Like for instance if I was tempted to shape something too much, to shape something so it was no longer accurate, no longer truthful, I would immediately envisage a horrific future.
Right.  You play out a worst-case scenario in your head.
Exactly.  Where it begins with Twitter, and it ends with, you know, jumping off a building.

And that gets back to what we were saying earlier though, where a psychopath, or someone that doesn't have those built-in social meters and thresholds is gonna be capable of doing things that people like us won't be.
Yes.

And you're editing yourself in a way to limit your own anxiety.  I do the same thing.  I have a very similar process where I'm always thinking about my actions and projecting then into the future.  And it happens very seamlessly, right?  You don't actually have to put a lot of energy into it.  It's just part of your, the way your brain works.

Yeah, absolutely.  It's "what-if" scenarios that haunt people with OCD and so on.  Yes.  Psychopaths don't have that, which makes me suspect that psychopathy is the most pleasant feeling of all the mental disorders.  So all of the things that keep us good, anxiety, guilt, remorse and so on, is, am I right in saying, Steven, shift to the amygdala and the central nervous system.

Yeah, well, the amygdala is part of the central nervous system.  But you mean, the frontal cortex is where all of the social mores are, the social morals, the things that give you anxiety so that you internally police yourself and you don't do things because you're afraid of social humiliation.  That emotion exists so that we can exist in a society.  And in fact what social psychology is showing is that people will essentially cheat exactly as much as they think they'll get away with.  And it is, more than anyone else, the fear of social humiliation that keeps us from doing things which are inherently greedy or self-serving.  We are totally self-serving unless we think that other people's perception of us being self-serving is no longer in our best interest.  So it's ultimately still self-serving.
There's something so unraveling about that.

But that's, we're chimpanzees; that's how we behave.  Just in a very sophisticated way.  But then again in psychopaths they sort of lack that . . . it must be very freeing.  I think that's why they're very charismatic, very compelling characters, 'cause it's like, wow, imagine having the freedom to just really do whatever you want .
And so difficult to treat, too, because there's no incentive to change.  People with anxiety disorders want to get better.

That ties into what you were saying about not liking the haughtiness of skepticism.  And that's, I think, one of the challenges that we have.  It's hard to tell people they're wrong about something without coming off as being haughty.  So . . .

I mean the way I get away with it is to be very open about my own irrationalities; my anxieties; and people can sort of connect to that, on a sort of flawed level, I guess.  People connect to me on a flawed level, and I think that helps.  And, I think, yeah, that's a good way around that, is to be . . . . but you do that, Steven.  You talk about everybody's rationality.
Yeah.
You don't say skeptics are perfect.
No, no.
And that's very likable to do that.

I don't think anyone really does that.  I think it's an inadvertent thing that it comes across . . . I think people are looking for a reason to dismiss what the skeptics are saying because they don't like the conclusions.  Like, oh, you're just being closed minded and haughty, and it's kind of a cheap shot, I think, oftentimes.
Yes.

I do think that skeptics have evolved as a community to the point where we realize that that finger-wagging, haughty skeptic is completely ineffectual.   If we wanna actually change people's minds.  And in fact it's not even really true that, you know . . . we are all irrational.  It's a matter of having a process that deals with that and understanding it.
JR.  Yeah.  Also, you talked at the beginning about this kind of humiliation idea, and the more open you are about your weaknesses and so on, the less humiliatable you are.
Yeah, yeah . . .
It's like, these things kind of only exist when you're keeping them a secret, keeping them in the darkness.

It is all part of the human narrative, right?  So I think that's what you're, Jon, excellent at, as an investigative journalist and a writer, is making your, you are a good storyteller, and the are very human, and you're very much in the stories.  But the process comes out, in that, still.

Yeah.  But to me . . . I think this, where I disagreed with what you said was the I think self-deception, so these kind of more serious aspects of things, not the kind of, let's say for want of a better phrase, the sort of, the confirmation bias you find in the corpse instead of the confirmation bias you find in a haunted honty-tonk . . . I actually think people really are interested in this, 'cause I think psychology books are really popular and, you know, Richard Wiseman's books sell a lot of copies, and I think people do want to know about their own
Yeah
flawed thought processes, actually.  I think.  Pleasure to see you all in the flesh.  It's strange to actually hear these voices coming out of actual human faces.  (laughter)
We do have actual human faces.
We've shattered your illusion apparently.  (laughter)
Thanks, Jon.
Thank you.

sections.title: Science or Fiction

sections.text: Each week I come up with three science news items or facts, two genuine and one fictitious and I challenge my panel of skeptics to tell me which one is the fake.  You guys ready for this week?
We are ready.
Time to play.
You'll find these are interesting.
Always.

Here we go.  Item number one.  Scientists have developed an imaging system that can look through walls into a burning building and identify survivors that need rescuing.  Item number two.  A new analysis finds that Spiderman’s webbing would have been strong enough to stop the commuter trains as depicted in the Spiderman 2 movie.  And item number three.  Researchers discover a virus with an adaptive immune system.
Wow.
Jay, you spoke first, so you get to go first.
The first one about scientists developing an imaging system that can look through walls into a burning building.
Let me guess.  Google glasses.
